passages.t: ‘I am the LORD’: God's answer and his promises
passages.happening:
God answers Moses' complaint: “Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh, for because of My mighty hand he will let the people go; because of My strong hand he will drive them out of his land” (verse 1).

“God also told Moses, ‘I am the LORD. I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob as God Almighty, but by My name the LORD I did not make Myself known to them’” (verses 2-3). He made a covenant with them to give them Canaan, and now he has heard Israel's groaning “and I have remembered My covenant” (verses 4-5).

“Therefore tell the Israelites: ‘I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under the yoke of the Egyptians and deliver you from their bondage. I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with mighty acts of judgment. I will take you as My own people, and I will be your God’” (verses 6-7). Then they will know that he is the LORD their God. And he will bring them into the land he swore to give to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Moses asked ‘why?’ at the end of chapter 5. God does not scold him, and he does not explain the delay either. He tells Moses who he is and what he will do. ‘Now you will see’ answers ‘why?’ with a promise of sight, not a reason.

Listen to how the speech is built. It opens with ‘I am the LORD’. The words come again at the start of the promises in verse 6, and they close the speech in verse 8. That was how a king opened a decree, with his name. In between, God is the one who acts in every sentence: I appeared, I made my covenant, I have heard, I have remembered, I will bring you out, I will deliver, I will redeem, I will take, I will bring you in, I will give. Israel does nothing in this speech but receive.

‘Redeem’ is a word from family law. The redeemer was the nearest male relative. If a man sold himself into slavery because he was poor, his relative was to buy him back. If he sold his family land, his relative was to buy it back. When God says ‘I will redeem you’, he is acting as Israel's next of kin. This is the first time the Bible uses this word for God's act toward Israel.

‘An outstretched arm’ answers Egypt's own pictures. From very early times Egyptian art showed Pharaoh with his arm raised to strike down his enemies, and royal inscriptions praised the king's mighty arm. Here the arm that saves belongs to the LORD, and it will be raised against Pharaoh.

‘I will take you as My own people, and I will be your God’ is the heart of the covenant. The verb ‘take’ is the one used for taking a wife. The rescue is for belonging. Israel is set free from Egypt in order to belong to God.

Later Jewish tradition tied the four cups of wine at the Passover meal to the promises of verses 6 and 7: I will bring you out, I will deliver you, I will redeem you, I will take you. Jewish families still drink those four cups each year as they remember.
passages.later:
The promise ‘I will be your God, and you will be my people’ runs through the whole Bible. Jeremiah promises a new covenant in the same words: “I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they will be My people” (Jeremiah 31:33). And Revelation ends with it: “They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God” (Revelation 21:3).

The New Testament uses the word ‘redeem’ for what Christ has done. God sent his Son “to redeem those under the law, that we might receive our adoption as sons” (Galatians 4:5). Christ “gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for Himself a people for His own possession” (Titus 2:14).
passages.hard:
God says, ‘by My name the LORD I did not make Myself known to them’. Yet Genesis uses the name often. God himself says to Abraham, “I am the LORD, who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans” (Genesis 15:7), and people call on the name as early as Genesis 4:26. How do these fit?

Three main answers are given. Many critical scholars see two traditions here. One, usually called the priestly source, held that the name was first made known to Moses. Another assumed it was known from the beginning. The final editor let both stand.

Many traditional Jewish and Christian interpreters, among them the medieval Jewish commentator Rashi, argue that to ‘know’ a name in the Bible means to know by experience what it stands for. The patriarchs used the name, but they lived by promises they never saw kept. Israel is about to learn what the name means as God keeps those promises. On this reading the verse sets two stages of knowing side by side.

A third, smaller group notes that the writer of Genesis, telling the story after Sinai, may have used the name for the God the patriarchs knew as God Almighty.

Each view takes the text seriously. They differ on how the five books came together and on what it means to know a name. These notes do not choose. The chapter's own claim is clear: the God who speaks is the God who promised Abraham, now making himself known in a new way.
passages.asks: God answered Moses' ‘why?’ not with a reason but with himself: ‘I am the LORD’. Ask whether you can trust God when he does not explain. And ask what it would mean for you to know God, not only by name, but by seeing him keep his word.

passages.happening:
“Moses relayed this message to the Israelites, but on account of their broken spirit and cruel bondage, they did not listen to him” (verse 9).

God tells Moses to go to Pharaoh again. Moses replies, “If the Israelites will not listen to me, then why would Pharaoh listen to me, since I am unskilled in speech?” (verse 12).

“Then the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron and gave them a charge concerning both the Israelites and Pharaoh king of Egypt, to bring the Israelites out of the land of Egypt” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
For the first time in Exodus a word from God does not bring faith. The people who believed and worshiped in 4:31 are now too crushed to hear.

The Hebrew for ‘broken spirit’ means shortness of breath. It describes someone worn down to the point of despair, who has no breath left even to hope. Notice that the text explains their failure. It does not condemn it. Their spirit was crushed by cruel work. The God who heard their groaning understands why they cannot listen now.

Moses' answer is an argument from the smaller to the larger: if my own people will not listen, how will Pharaoh? In Hebrew he calls his lips ‘uncircumcised’, a picture of lips closed off and unfit for their task. The BSB puts it ‘unskilled in speech’.

God does not argue. He simply gives his command again, to both brothers.
passages.later:
The psalms know this kind of despair and still bring it to God: “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit” (Psalm 34:18).

Jeremiah uses the same Hebrew word for ears that will not hear. The BSB puts it this way: “their ears are closed, so they cannot hear” (Jeremiah 6:10).
passages.asks: The people could not listen because their spirits were crushed. Ask whether you know someone too worn down to hear good news, and how you could be patient with them. And ask whether, in your own hard seasons, you have let God keep speaking even when you could not take it in.

passages.happening:
“These were the heads of their fathers’ houses” (verse 14). The list begins with Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, and Simeon, and then slows down at Levi: “These were the names of the sons of Levi according to their records: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Levi lived 137 years” (verse 16).

Kohath's son Amram “married his father’s sister Jochebed, and she bore him Aaron and Moses” (verse 20). The list names Aaron's wife Elisheba and their four sons, Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar (verse 23), Korah and his sons (verses 21, 24), and Aaron's grandson Phinehas (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
The story stops for a family list. It can seem like an odd place for one, but it has a purpose.

The list starts as if it will name all twelve sons of Jacob, Reuben first and Simeon second. But it stops at Levi, the third son, because Levi is the point. This is the family of Moses and Aaron. Moses has just doubted himself. The list answers by showing where he comes from, and who the men are who will speak to Pharaoh.

Many of the names come back later. The three sons of Levi became the three groups of Levites who carried the tabernacle (Numbers 3 and 4). Nadab and Abihu died for offering fire God had not commanded (Leviticus 10:1-2). Korah, a first cousin of Moses, led a rebellion against him (Numbers 16). His family survived, and ‘the sons of Korah’ appear in the headings of several psalms. Phinehas became known for his zeal (Numbers 25). Phinehas is an Egyptian name, meaning ‘the Nubian’. It is one of several Egyptian names in this family, Moses' own among them, that fit a family living in Egypt.

Aaron's wife Elisheba came from the leading family of Judah; her brother Nahshon led that tribe. In Greek her name is Elizabeth.

Two things here raise questions. Amram married his father's sister. The text records it without comment, though the law given later at Sinai forbids such a marriage (Leviticus 18:12). And the years given for Kohath and Amram cannot fill the 430 years of Israel's stay in Egypt if each name is father to son. Many interpreters think the list names the heads of clans and skips generations, as biblical lists often do. Others link its four generations from Levi to Moses with God's word to Abraham that his family would return ‘in the fourth generation’ (Genesis 15:16).
passages.later:
The later law forbids Amram's marriage: “You must not have sexual relations with your father’s sister” (Leviticus 18:12).

Korah's rebellion is told in Numbers: “Now Korah son of Izhar, the son of Kohath son of Levi” rose against Moses (Numbers 16:1).

Matthew names Nahshon, Elisheba's brother, among the ancestors of Jesus (Matthew 1:4). And Luke tells of a priest Zechariah, “whose wife Elizabeth was a daughter of Aaron” (Luke 1:5). These are links of family history, not prophecy.
passages.asks: God answers Moses' doubt by reminding him of his family, a long line of ordinary people, some faithful, some not. Ask what in your own family's story God might use, and what he might redeem. And ask whether you believe God can work through a family as mixed as Levi's.

passages.happening:
“It was this Aaron and Moses to whom the LORD said, ‘Bring the Israelites out of the land of Egypt by their divisions.’ Moses and Aaron were the ones who spoke to Pharaoh king of Egypt in order to bring the Israelites out of Egypt” (verses 26-27).

On the day God spoke to Moses in Egypt, he said, “I am the LORD; tell Pharaoh king of Egypt everything I say to you” (verse 29). Moses replies again, “Since I am unskilled in speech, why would Pharaoh listen to me?” (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
These verses tell the reader why the list was there. This is the Aaron and Moses, these very men, whom God sent. Aaron is named first in verse 26, because he is the older. Moses is named first in verse 27, because of his role.

‘By their divisions’ is a military word, used for an army in ranks. Israel will leave Egypt not as a mob of runaways, but as the LORD's army.

Then the story picks up exactly where it paused in verse 12. Moses' objection is repeated almost word for word. This is a way Hebrew stories have of saying: we are back where we left off. The next chapter gives God's answer.
passages.later:
Exodus 12 uses the same military word when Israel leaves: “all the LORD’s divisions went out of the land of Egypt” (Exodus 12:41).

The psalm remembers these two brothers as God's chosen servants: “He sent Moses His servant, and Aaron, whom He had chosen” (Psalm 105:26).
passages.asks: Moses kept saying that he could not speak, and God kept sending him anyway. Ask what you keep repeating to God as a reason you cannot do what he asks. And ask whether it might be time to stop repeating it, and go.
